_comment: Adjudications of spec-probe findings. A finding is not a defect until somebody has read it.
The gate this file serves does NOT block on findings. It blocks on findings NOBODY HAS READ.
That is the only defensible shape given the measured precision: over eight built families the
probe produced 23 findings and independent adversarial review refuted all 23, so a blocking
gate would have blocked the entire portfolio on noise, and a gate that blocks everything gets
switched off. A gate that demands a written reason costs one read per finding and cannot be

Nine of the original 23 findings are absent from this file because they were not judgement calls
at all - they were bugs in the probe, which the adjudication exposed and which are now fixed:
rule codes read out of a keyed lookup table as if source order were evaluation order; constants
read out of scenario generators and build-time self-gates, neither of which grades a subject; and
a disjunction of two acceptable methods reported as two separate mandatory calls.

adjudications.reason: The obligation to call `currentPolicy` on every attempt is stated three times over in visible text, including for the blocking path. SPEC.md:87 opens the Audit Contract with "Every decision must have an audit event with:" and SPEC.md:91 requires "observed current policy id, generation, status, per-spend limit and daily limit, or null when missing" — and SPEC.md:63-65 says `authority.currentPolicy(id)` ... "are the only current authority interface", so the only way to obtain those observed values is the call. The blocking-vs-granting scope objection is closed by the visible starter, which refuses every request (starter/subject.mjs:29-30 `const allowed = false; const reason = "DWS1_CURRENT_POLICY_REQUIRED"`) and still calls the facade unconditionally at starter/subject.mjs:20 `const policy = authority.currentPolicy(view.request.policyId);`, with starter/subject.mjs:25 instructing "reconcile the four current facts above and decide the spend from them". Per-attempt is settled by SPEC.md:47-48 ("The current authority state is rebuilt for each attempt") plus SPEC.md:58-59, which permits cross-attempt in-memory state "only to prevent duplicate wallet effects for the same idempotency key" — so carrying an earlier attempt's observation forward instead of re-calling is explicitly disallowed.

This is the most explicitly stated of the four: SPEC.md:96 requires in every decision's audit event (SPEC.md:87) "observed remaining budget returned by the facade, or null when unavailable" — the phrase "returned by the facade" names the call itself, so the value cannot be supplied from the cached snapshot or the subject-owned claim (which does carry a `remainingBudget` field, types.ts:80, and is barred as authority by SPEC.md:29 and DWS7 at SPEC.md:77). SPEC.md:64 lists `authority.remainingBudget(walletId, owner)` in "the only current authority interface". The block-path scope objection fails again on the visible skeleton, which refuses everything yet calls starter/subject.mjs:23 `const remainingBudget = authority.remainingBudget(view.request.walletId, view.request.owner);` unconditionally, under starter/subject.mjs:25's instruction to "reconcile the four current facts above". Per-attempt re-observation is fixed by SPEC.md:47-48 and the SPEC.md:58-59 restriction of retained state to duplicate-effect prevention only.

The hidden check at verify.ts:65-72 requires each attempt to call currentAlias, evalStream and baseline, and the visible SPEC states that obligation directly and adjudicates its boundary. SPEC.md:66 says 'The rules below are decided from `currentAlias`, `evalStream` and `baseline`.' and SPEC.md:74 (DMD1) says 'A rollout decision must reconcile the current alias mapping from the rollout facade.' The adjudicating sentence is SPEC.md:67-68, which singles out the one facade method that is NOT graded: '`rolloutLedger(alias)` returns the append-only alias-mapping history for context; no rule in this SPEC reads it and the verifier does not require the call.' — by naming the exception it settles that the other three reads are required, and verify.ts:61-64 carries the matching comment. The per-attempt scope is also covered: SPEC.md:46 says 'The current rollout state is rebuilt for each attempt' and SPEC.md:56-57 permits cross-call memory 'only to prevent duplicate effects for the same idempotency key', which forecloses reusing a prior attempt's observations instead of re-reading.

The probe anchored on policy.ts:28, which sits inside the `REASON_CODES` string-literal array (policy.ts:26-36) — an enumeration of code names used only to derive `type ReasonCode = (typeof REASON_CODES)[number]` at policy.ts:37, and never consulted for ordering anywhere in src/. The actual first-match-wins order is the control flow of `decide()` (policy.ts:119-211): P8 (l.122) → P7 (l.136) → P1 (l.143) → P2 (l.152) → P6 (l.160) → P4 (l.171) → P3 (l.186/193) → P5 (l.204). That is precisely the visible table in SPEC.md:24-31, which reads row-for-row `| 1 | P8_UNKNOWN_TOOL |`, `| 2 | P7_TOOL_OUTPUT_AUTHORITY |`, `| 3 | P1_UNTRUSTED_AUTHORITY |`, `| 4 | P2_CAPABILITY_NOT_GRANTED |`, `| 5 | P6_APPROVAL_MISMATCH |`, `| 6 | P4_UNTRUSTED_SCOPE_EXPANSION |`, `| 7 | P3_SCOPE_VIOLATION |`, `| 8 | P5_SECRET_EGRESS |` — and it cannot drift, because src/challenge/package.ts:128 renders that table from the same `RULES` array (policy.ts:46-87) whose order matches `decide()`. Precedence is also stated in words at SPEC.md:3-4: "Eight rules, evaluated **in this order**. A call violating several is attributed to the first it hits, so your reason code is comparable to the grader's expectation." Both clauses of the finding are therefore false: the quoted order is not a precedence, and precedence is stated. (One unrelated nuance the probe did not raise: policy.ts:125-132 returns P1 for a nonexistent authorizing segment ahead of the P7 check — not the claim as filed, and unreachable for well-formed scenarios.)

The claimed order does not differ from the visible order — it is identical. The probe anchored on the hidden `RULES` array (policy.ts:61-94), whose sequence is M0, M1, M2, M3, M4, M5, M6, M7; SPEC.md's rule table publishes exactly that sequence, numbered 1-8: `| 1 | \`M0_UNKNOWN_TOOL\` |` (line 58), `| 2 | \`M1_UNTRUSTED_AUTHORITY\` |` (line 59), `| 3 | \`M2_CAPABILITY_NOT_GRANTED\` |` (line 60), `| 4 | \`M3_UNTRUSTED_ARGUMENT\` |` (line 61), `| 5 | \`M4_UNPROVENANCED_RECALL\` |` (line 62). And the precedence is not merely implied by table position, it is stated normatively at SPEC.md:3-4: "Eight rules, evaluated **in this order**. A call violating several is attributed to the first it hits, so your reason code is comparable to the grader's expectation." I also checked the one place `decide()` departs from array order — it evaluates the M3/M5 branch (policy.ts:214-228) before the M4 loop (policy.ts:229-231) — and confirmed it is unobservable: M5 requires a resolved arg with an untrusted trust level, which requires a canonical record with non-empty provenance, while M4 requires `provenance.length === 0`; the generator sets provenance uniformly per scenario via `prov()` (scenarios.ts:172), so no generated call can ever hold both a provenanced-untrusted arg and an unprovenanced arg. The remaining M3-vs-M5 tie-break, the only one that could bite, is spelled out verbatim in the visible rules at SPEC.md:61 and SPEC.md:63.

SPEC.md:10 states the rule normatively: "`R4_CONFIRMATION_OBSERVED` | A step whose target declares `data-opens-confirmation` must not complete until a confirmation has been observed and accepted. An absent dialog is not a confirmation." The facade block at SPEC.md:52 lists `confirmationPresent() -> boolean` and types.ts:116-117 names it as the observe primitive: "/** Observe whether a confirmation is currently presented. */ confirmationPresent: () => boolean;" — R4 keeps "observed" and "accepted" as two distinct conjuncts and the facade supplies exactly one method for each (`confirmationPresent`, `acceptConfirmation`), so the observation act is adjudicated to `confirmationPresent`, reinforced by the `confirmationObserved` audit field at types.ts:134. The hidden gate at verify.ts:149-153 is strictly narrower than R4 (only irreversible steps that actually ran against a live node carrying `data-opens-confirmation: "true"`), so it does not over-reach the stated scope. The one competing reading — inferring presence from `acceptConfirmation()` throwing (SPEC.md:53) — rests on a descriptive facade note, not normative text, and collapses a conjunction the SPEC deliberately keeps split; it is too weak to defeat SPEC.md:10.

SPEC.md:7 states the rule normatively: "`R1_SELECTOR_RESOLVED_LIVE` | Every step's selector must be resolved against the live tree at replay time. The recorded node id is a hint, not an address." The facade block at SPEC.md:49 lists `query(selector) -> { node, matches, pending }` and types.ts:109-110 documents it as "/** Resolve a selector against the LIVE tree, right now. */ query: (selector: Selector) => QueryResult;" — it is the only facade operation that accepts a selector, so there is no second reading of how to satisfy R1. The only alternative (act on `recordedNodeId` via `attr`/`click`) is explicitly foreclosed by the same SPEC line calling the recorded id "a hint, not an address", and the starter at starter/subject.mjs:16-17 already calls `app.query(step.selector)` under the comment "TODO: resolve the selector LIVE." The hidden check fires only when steps are reported as run with ZERO query calls, which is exactly an R1 violation, not a stricter unstated obligation.

The probe misread a disjunction as a mandatory call. verify.ts:264 is `const queries = calls.filter((c) => c.method === "query" || c.method === "queryAnchor").length;` and the only failure it feeds is `if (claimedRuns > 0 && queries === 0)` at verify.ts:266 — so `queryAnchor` is never individually required; calling `query` alone satisfies it entirely. The obligation the check actually enforces (look at the live tree before claiming a step ran) is stated verbatim: SPEC.md:79 `L1_RESOLVE_LIVE` — "Resolve each step's selector against the LIVE tree at replay time. `step.recordedNodeId` is a hint, not an address", reinforced at SPEC.md:112 "`Observed` means the subject made the facade call that exposes the live fact during this replay pass". Both facade calls are published at SPEC.md:231-232 and types.ts:179-180.

verify.ts:259 is `if (call.detail.includes("advanced=false")) stopped = true;`, the latch for the stall check at verify.ts:252-257. The literal token and the rule built on it are both printed in the visible package. SPEC.md:86 `L8_SETTLE_BUDGET`: "`settle()` advances one logical tick and returns `{advanced, remaining}`. ... Once `advanced: false` comes back the clock has stopped; calling `settle()` again is a stall and is graded as one." types.ts:146 repeats it: "One logical tick. `advanced: false` means the clock has stopped; asking again is a stall." Nothing is left for the subject to guess — the sentinel value, the polarity, and the grading consequence are all stated.

`queriedIds` (verify.ts:94-98) splits the ledger detail on " -> " and returns the ids a query RESOLVED, not the selector the subject typed — app.ts:808-813 and 824-827 record `... -> id+id`. So verify.ts:308 does not require the subject to know or type the string "dlg"; it requires that some earlier query/queryAnchor in the same pass actually resolved the alertdialog root (app.ts:937-938 builds `dlg` with role `alertdialog`). That is exactly the visible rule: SPEC.md:81 `L3_CONFIRMATION_OBSERVED` — "mounts a `role=\"alertdialog\"` node. Find that node in the tree, then `acceptConfirmation(<its Confirm button's id>)`. Assuming the id is not observing the dialog." SPEC.md:115-117 adjudicates the narrower reading too (finding only the button is insufficient): "For a confirmation, observation is resolving the mounted `alertdialog` node and then accepting its Confirm button by id."
